techniques.name: Factor Analysis
techniques.description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team finds that forty macroeconomic and credit-bureau inputs to a default-risk model are heavily correlated. Exploratory factor analysis groups them into four factors the team can name, such as growth, inflation, household debt and credit conditions, and the model is rebuilt on the factor scores so its drivers can be explained to the risk committee in four terms instead of forty.

A flood-forecasting team with sixty correlated gauge, soil-moisture and satellite inputs runs factor analysis on the training data to find a few underlying drivers, such as rainfall intensity, catchment wetness and river level. Forecast explanations are then reported per driver, which operators can relate to what they see on the ground.

limitations.description: The standard model is linear, with each variable a weighted sum of factors plus noise. Maximum-likelihood extraction also assumes roughly normal data, so skewed, binary or strongly non-linear variables can distort the loadings. Check distributions first, or choose an extraction method that does not require normality.

Factors are statistical summaries of correlation, not discovered causes. A factor labelled 'economic confidence' is the analyst's reading of which variables load together, and a different rotation or sample may support a different label.

Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which have no single correct answer and can change both which variables group together and how readable the factors are. Report the choices made and check that the structure is stable.
Requires a sample that is large relative to the number of variables. With small samples the loadings are unstable and change when a few cases are added or removed.

Describes the structure of the data fed into it, not how a trained model uses that data. Factors of a model's inputs say nothing about which factors the model relies on, unless the model is also built on or analysed with the factor scores.

Overview and confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis of AI literacy scale
resources.abstract: Comprehensive concepts of AI literacy (AIL) and valid measures are essential for research (e.g., intervention studies) and practice (e.g., personnel selection/development) alike. To date, several scales have been published, sharing standard features but differing in some aspects. We first aim to briefly overview instruments identified from unsystematic literature research in February 2023. We identified four scales and one collection of items. We describe the instruments and compare them. We identified common themes and overlaps in the instruments and developmental procedure. We also found differences regarding scale development procedures and latent dimensions. Following this literature research, we came to the conclusion that the literature on AI literacy measurement was fragmented, and little effort was undertaken to integrate different AI literacy conceptualizations. The second focus of this study is to test the factorial structures of existing AIL measurement instruments and identify latent dimensions of AIL across all instruments. We used robust maximum-likelihood confirmatory factor analysis to test factorial structures in a joint survey of all AIL items in an English-speaking online sample ( N =219). We found general support for all instruments' factorial structures with minor deviations from the original factorial structures for some of the instruments. In a second analysis step, to address the issue of fragmented research on AI literacy conceptualization and measurement, we used principal axis exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation to identify latent dimensions across all items. We found four correlated latent dimensions of AIL, which were mostly interpretable as the abilities to use and interact with AI, to design/program AI (incl. in-depth technical knowledge), to perform complex cognitive operations regarding AI (e.g., ethical considerations), and a common factor for the abilities to detect AI/differentiate between AI and humans and manage persuasive influences of AI (i.e., persuasion literacy). Our findings sort the multitude of AIL instruments and reveal four latent core dimensions of AIL. Thus, they contribute importantly to the conceptual understanding of AIL that has been fragmented so far. • We give an overview of AI literacy measures. • Their factorial structures were mostly confirmed. • PA EFA identified four correlated latent dimensions across all instruments.

sample_claims.text: The default-risk model's correlated inputs reduce to a small number of named factors that account for most of their shared variance, so its drivers can be explained at factor level.
The flood-forecasting inputs group into a few factors whose loadings domain experts recognise as physically meaningful drivers.
The number of factors retained, the extraction method and the rotation are documented, and the factor structure is stable when the analysis is repeated on a separate sample.

techniques.name: Principal Component Analysis
techniques.description: Principal Component Analysis transforms high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation by finding the directions (principal components) that capture the maximum variance in the data. Each component is a linear combination of original features, with the first component explaining the most variance, the second component the most remaining variance orthogonal to the first, and so on. This technique reveals underlying patterns in data structure, enables visualisation of complex datasets, and helps identify which combinations of features drive the most variation in the data.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing customer behavior data with dozens of variables (purchase frequency, spending patterns, demographics) to identify the 2-3 main dimensions that explain customer segmentation, revealing whether customers cluster by spending level, product preferences, or shopping frequency.

Reducing dimensionality of image data for facial recognition systems by finding the principal components that capture the most variation in face shapes and expressions, helping understand which facial features contribute most to distinguishing between individuals.

limitations.description: Principal components are abstract linear combinations of original features that often lack clear real-world interpretation or meaning.
Only captures linear relationships between features, missing non-linear patterns and complex interactions in the data.
Results are highly sensitive to feature scaling - features with larger numerical ranges can dominate the principal components.
Information loss is inherent when reducing dimensions, and choosing the optimal number of components requires balancing simplicity with retained variance.

resources.title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

sample_claims.text: The feature space reveals latent factors that explain correlated environmental measurements without relying on predetermined variable groupings
The model's high-dimensional patient data is reducible to a small number of orthogonal patterns that capture most variation in clinical measurements
The financial indicators decompose into uncorrelated variance components that reveal which measurement combinations drive portfolio risk
The image representation preserves maximal variance through linear transformations that identify which pixel combinations distinguish between object categories
The customer behavior measurements organize into ordered variance patterns showing which feature combinations best separate distinct market segments

techniques.name: UMAP
techniques.description: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that creates 2D or 3D visualisations of high-dimensional data by constructing a mathematical model of the data's underlying manifold structure. Unlike t-SNE, UMAP preserves both local neighbourhood relationships and global topology more effectively, using techniques from topological data analysis and Riemannian geometry. This approach often produces more interpretable cluster layouts while maintaining meaningful distances between clusters, making it particularly valuable for exploratory data analysis and understanding complex dataset structures.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing single-cell RNA sequencing data to visualise how different cell types cluster based on gene expression patterns, revealing developmental trajectories and identifying previously unknown cell subtypes in tissue samples.

Exploring customer segmentation by reducing hundreds of behavioural and demographic features to 2D space, showing how different customer groups relate to each other and identifying transition zones where customers might move between segments.

limitations.description: Hyperparameter choices (n_neighbors, min_dist, metric) significantly influence the embedding structure and can lead to very different interpretations of the same data.
While preserving global structure better than t-SNE, distances in the reduced space still don't directly correspond to distances in the original feature space.
Performance can be sensitive to the choice of distance metric, which may not be obvious for complex or mixed data types.
Like other manifold learning techniques, it assumes the data lies on a lower-dimensional manifold, which may not hold for all datasets.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction
resources.abstract: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a novel manifold learning technique for dimension reduction. UMAP is constructed from a theoretical framework based in Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology. The result is a practical scalable algorithm that applies to real world data. The UMAP algorithm is competitive with t-SNE for visualization quality, and arguably preserves more of the global structure with superior run time performance. Furthermore, UMAP has no computational restrictions on embedding dimension, making it viable as a general purpose dimension reduction technique for machine learning.

resources.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
resources.abstract: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is a dimension reduction technique that can be used for visualisation similarly to t-SNE, but also for general non-linear dimension reduction. UMAP has a rigorous mathematical foundation, but is simple to use, with a scikit-learn compatible API. UMAP is among the fastest manifold learning implementations available -significantly faster than most t-SNE implementations.

Dimensionality reduction for visualizing single-cell data using UMAP
resources.abstract: Advances in single-cell technologies have enabled high-resolution dissection of tissue composition. Several tools for dimensionality reduction are available to analyze the large number of parameters generated in single-cell studies. Recently, a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), was developed for the analysis of any type of high-dimensional data. Here we apply it to biological data, using three well-characterized mass cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Comparing the performance of UMAP with five other tools, we find that UMAP provides the fastest run times, highest reproducibility and the most meaningful organization of cell clusters. The work highlights the use of UMAP for improved visualization and interpretation of single-cell data.

resources.title: Dimensionality reduction by UMAP to visualize physical and genetic interactions
resources.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is often used to visualize complex expression profiling data. Here, we use the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) method on published transcript profiles of 1484 single gene deletions of Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Proximity in low-dimensional UMAP space identifies groups of genes that correspond to protein complexes and pathways, and finds novel protein interactions, even within well-characterized complexes. This approach is more sensitive than previous methods and should be broadly useful as additional transcriptome datasets become available for other organisms.

sample_claims.text: The high-dimensional dataset's underlying cluster relationships are visualized while preserving meaningful distances between distinct groups
The data visualization reveals both local neighborhood patterns and global topology without sacrificing one for the other
The model's learned representations can be explored through low-dimensional projections that preserve the manifold structure of the original feature space
Complex dataset structures with non-linear relationships are comprehensible through two-dimensional visualizations that maintain topological fidelity

techniques.name: Sequential CART Synthesis
techniques.description: Sequential CART synthesis creates an artificial copy of a confidential microdata set (records about individual people or organisations) that can be released in place of the real data, in the form used by the synthpop package for R. Variables are synthesised one at a time in a chosen order: the first is generated by sampling with replacement from its observed values, and for each later variable a classification or regression tree (CART) is fitted on the real data to predict it from the variables earlier in the order. Each synthetic record is passed down that tree using its already-synthesised values, and the new value is copied from a randomly chosen real record in the leaf it reaches, so the joint distribution of the data is rebuilt as a chain of conditional distributions. Disclosure risk is limited by setting a minimum leaf size, smoothing synthesised continuous values and removing synthetic records that reproduce unique real ones, and several synthetic copies can be released so that analysts can allow for the extra uncertainty that synthesis adds.

example_use_cases.description: A national longitudinal study that links census returns to administrative records such as births, deaths and cancer registrations for a sample of the population cannot let approved researchers take the data off site. Its support team runs CART synthesis to produce a bespoke synthetic extract for each project, so researchers can explore the data and write and test their analysis code at their own institution before the final model is run on the real data in the secure setting.

A hospital trust wants a university team to develop a readmission model without receiving patient records. It releases a CART-synthesised copy of the admissions table with a minimum leaf size of ten and kernel smoothing of continuous values, removes any synthetic record that matches a unique real patient on age, sex and postcode district, and runs a disclosure-risk assessment before release.

A national statistics office publishes a synthetic teaching file of its labour force survey for university courses, generated by sequential CART synthesis with the variable order and minimum leaf sizes chosen with subject experts, and labels every record as synthetic so that no reader mistakes a row for a real respondent.

limitations.description: It gives no formal privacy guarantee. No synthetic record is a real person, but trees can reproduce rare combinations and extreme values, and an intruder who knows that a real record holds the largest value of a variable can bound it from the synthetic maximum. Risk must be measured for each release and reduced with larger leaves, smoothing and removal of unique matches, each of which costs analytical value.

Relationships the trees miss disappear from the synthetic data. A tree grown from few records may never split on a variable that matters, so the synthetic data show no association where the real data have one; in the method's original evaluation a regression coefficient for sex was attenuated to zero in this way. Small subgroups and weak effects are the most exposed.

Results depend on the order in which variables are synthesised and on which earlier variables predict each later one. A careless order can produce impossible combinations, such as a detailed category that contradicts the summary variable derived from it, so detailed variables should be synthesised before derived ones and the output checked for inconsistencies.

Synthetic data cannot reproduce every analysis of the real data. Analyses the synthesiser did not plan for may give different answers, so a release should state which analyses it supports, and users should confirm key findings on the real data, for example through a verification service or secure access.

resources.title: synthpop: Bespoke Creation of Synthetic Data in R
resources.abstract: In many contexts, confidentiality constraints severely restrict access to unique and valuable microdata. Synthetic data which mimic the original observed data and preserve the relationships between variables but do not contain any disclosive records are one possible solution to this problem. The synthpop package for R, introduced in this paper, provides routines to generate synthetic versions of original data sets. We describe the methodology and its consequences for the data characteristics. We illustrate the package features using a survey data example.

resources.title: synthpop: Generating Synthetic Versions of Sensitive Microdata for Statistical Disclosure Control
resources.abstract: A tool for producing synthetic versions of microdata containing confidential information so that they are safe to be released to users for exploratory analysis. The key objective of generating synthetic data is to replace sensitive original values with synthetic ones causing minimal distortion of the statistical information contained in the data set. Variables, which can be categorical or continuous, are synthesised one-by-one using sequential modelling. Replacements are generated by drawing from conditional distributions fitted to the original data using parametric or classification and regression trees models. Data are synthesised via the function syn() which can be largely automated, if default settings are used, or with methods defined by the user. Optional parameters can be used to influence the disclosure risk and the analytical quality of the synthesised data. For a description of the implemented method see Nowok, Raab and Dibben (2016) <doi:10.18637/jss.v074.i11>. Functions to assess identity and attribute disclosure for the original and for the synthetic data are included in the package, and their use is illustrated in a vignette on disclosure (Practical Privacy Metrics for Synthetic Data).

resources.title: Using CART to Generate Partially Synthetic Public Use Microdata
resources.abstract: To limit disclosure risks, one approach is to release partially synthetic public use microdata sets. These comprise the units originally surveyed, but some collected values, for example sensitive values at high risk of disclosure or values of key identifiers, are replaced with multiple imputations. This article presents and evaluates the use of classification and regression trees to generate partially synthetic data. Two potential applications of CART are studied via simulation: (i) generate synthetic data for sensitive variables; and, (ii) generate synthetic data for variables that are key identifiers.

resources.title: Providing bespoke synthetic data for the UK Longitudinal Studies and other sensitive data with the synthpop package for R1
resources.abstract: Synthetic data methods were designed to address the conflicting demands placed on data holders to unlock the research and policy potential of microdata while at the same time preserving the confidentiality of individuals.Recently, these methods have become more widely recognized in the UK and the provision of bespoke synthetic data has been approved to expand the use of one of the UK Longitudinal Studies.The process of producing useful synthetic data involves, however, a substantial investment of research time, as it always requires some customising for the characteristics of an individual data set.At the same time, a substantial part of it can be automated and this is essential when the process has to be conducted rapidly and on a regular basis.This paper describes the application of synthetic data to the UK Longitudinal Studies, details implementation process for the Scottish Longitudinal Study and presents methods used in an R package synthpop that has been developed to facilitate production of non-disclosive entirely synthetic data.A reproducible example using open data is given to illustrate the synthesising procedure and to provide insights into quality of synthetic data generated using different automated approaches.

No confidential microdata left the secure environment during model development: external researchers wrote and tested their code on a synthetic extract, and only the final approved model was run on the real data.
A disclosure-risk assessment of the synthetic admissions table found no synthetic record matching a unique real patient on the agreed identifying variables.

techniques.name: Conditional Demographic Disparity
techniques.description: Conditional demographic disparity (CDD) measures whether members of a protected group make up a larger share of the people a system turns down than of the people it accepts, after taking into account a factor that differs between groups and that the assessor treats as a legitimate explanation of outcomes; Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell (2021) propose it as baseline statistical evidence for assessing possible discrimination under EU non-discrimination law. Demographic disparity is the group's share of the unfavourable outcomes minus its share of the favourable ones: in the Berkeley graduate admissions data the paper revisits, women were 46 per cent of rejected applicants but 32 per cent of admitted ones, a disparity of 0.14. CDD computes the same difference separately within each stratum of the conditioning attribute (there, the department applied to) and averages the strata, weighting each by its number of people, so a gap that arises only because groups apply in different proportions to strata with different acceptance rates (an instance of Simpson's paradox) drops out, while a gap within strata remains. Conditioning on department turns the Berkeley figure to about -0.02, a slight disparity in women's favour: within departments, women were on average 40 per cent of rejected and 42 per cent of admitted applicants. The output is the disparity in each stratum and their weighted average, computed on the outcomes recorded in a dataset before training or on a model's decisions after it; the authors present it as a descriptive magnitude to support a contextual judgement, not a pass-or-fail test, and the choice of conditioning attribute is a judgement the measure does not make.

example_use_cases.description: An employer's HR analytics team audits a CV-screening model used across job families. Women make up a larger share of screened-out applicants than of shortlisted ones overall, but apply in greater numbers to the families with the fewest vacancies per applicant, so the team reports CDD conditioned on job family, with each family's own disparity, letting the recruitment board see whether a gap remains within families before it decides whether to keep using the model.

A consumer lender's compliance team computes CDD on its credit model's decisions for applicants of different ethnic origins, recorded for equality monitoring, conditioned first on the loan product applied for and then on income band. It reports both results with the per-stratum figures and a written reason for treating each factor as a legitimate explanation, as the starting point for its assessment of possible indirect discrimination.

A local authority planning to train a model on past housing allocation decisions measures CDD in those decisions, conditioned on assessed band of housing need, before any training. A positive disparity for one ethnic group within need bands, larger than chance would explain, indicates that the labels carry a pattern a model could learn, and the project board uses the finding to decide whether those decisions can serve as training labels at all.

limitations.description: The result depends on which attribute is conditioned on, and the measure cannot tell whether that attribute is a legitimate explanation. If the attribute is itself shaped by discrimination, for instance if one group was deterred from applying to some departments, conditioning on it removes the very disparity a claimant would point to. Wachter et al. leave the choice of factors to courts and context, so each choice needs a recorded justification that a reviewer can contest.

The weighted average can hide large disparities of opposite sign in different strata. In the Berkeley data the per-department disparities run from about -0.09 to +0.05 around a summary of -0.02, and Wachter et al. note that the largest swings come from the department where few women applied, which chance alone could produce. A claim should rest on the per-stratum figures, with their counts, as well as on the summary.

Searching many conditioning attributes or their combinations will find disparities by chance, as the authors warn, and choosing among them after seeing the results can equally make a real one disappear. The authors also offer a descriptive magnitude rather than a statistical test, and set no threshold for how much disparity is too much, so the conditioning attributes need fixing before the data are examined, and a claim that a gap is real needs an interval or test added.

CDD compares shares of outcomes, not rates, so the same gap in acceptance rates gives a smaller value where the group is a small part of a stratum: accepted at 20 per cent against 50 per cent for others, a group scores about 0.33 where it is half the stratum but 0.02 where it is 2 per cent. A fixed threshold therefore tolerates larger rate gaps for smaller groups. Scores and graded outcomes must also first be cut into favourable and unfavourable, and the result changes with the cut.

In the open-source SageMaker Clarify code, a stratum where everyone gets the same outcome is counted rather than skipped: an all-rejected stratum adds a disparity equal to the group's share of it, though no one there was treated differently, so such strata need removing first. AWS has closed Clarify to new customers. The calculation is easy to reimplement, but published applications to deployed AI systems are scarce; the paper's worked example is the 1975 Berkeley admissions study.
